evidence: Title 'Frequent social media use could impact child development' maps to paper 310 (Carvalho & Ravindran, Journal of Research on Adolescence, 2025), which examines associations between social media hours and crystallized/fluid cognitive performance trajectories in ABCD youth. Published March 2025, article date March 2026. Paraphrase of social media effect on development/cognitive trajectories uniquely consistent with paper 310 among corpus papers on this topic published at that time.

Title 'Owning a smartphone at age 12 linked to mental and physical health risks' maps precisely to paper 431 (Barzilay et al., Pediatrics, 2026), which examines smartphone ownership and age of first smartphone acquisition as predictors of depression (OR=1.31), obesity (OR=1.40), and insufficient sleep (OR=1.62) in ABCD early adolescents. Mention of a specific age of acquisition and mental+physical health outcomes uniquely matches paper 431.

Title 'Social media use linked to cognitive decline in youth' maps to paper 1 (Nagata et al., JAMA 2025 — social media use trajectories and cognitive performance via NIH Toolbox) and paper 144 (Nagata et al., Lancet Regional Health-Americas 2026 — SM use trajectories and spatial/verbal memory). Both papers link social media to cognitive outcomes in ABCD youth. Article published November 2025, consistent with coverage of paper 1 (2025) and potentially paper 144 (preprint/early publication 2026). Multi-mapped to both.

Title 'Social Media Might Stunt Students' Intellect, Study Says' (U.S. News, Oct 14, 2025) maps to paper 1 (Nagata et al., JAMA 2025 — social media trajectories and cognitive performance including NIH Toolbox Cognition Battery subtests). Published in same October 2025 window as several outlets covering paper 1. 'Stunt intellect' paraphrases the finding of high-increasing SM trajectory associated with lower cognitive performance. Paper 310 (Carvalho 2025 fluid/crystallized) is alternative but paper 1 is higher-profile (JAMA) and more likely target of this framing.

exclusion_reason: out-of-corpus topic — article is about screen time and heart/cardiovascular health risks in youth; no corpus paper covers cardiovascular outcomes from smartphone/SM use
evidence: Title 'Youngsters Face Heart Health Risks From Too Much Screen Time' refers to a cardiovascular health outcome. No paper in candidate_papers.json covers heart health or cardiometabolic outcomes as a primary finding linked to smartphone/SM use. Paper 84 (Shou, Acta Psychologica — screen time + cognitive function + putamen volume, the provisional match) is unrelated to heart health. L1-L4 not met for any corpus paper.

exclusion_reason: general Nagata coverage — interview/highlight about smartphone use during school hours, a topic not specifically covered by any corpus paper; no paper from candidate_papers.json specifically examines in-school smartphone use as primary outcome
evidence: Title 'Jason Nagata, MD, MSc, highlights frequent teen smartphone use during school hours' describes an interview or editorial commentary about Nagata's work in general. No corpus paper specifically investigates smartphone use during school hours as a primary IV or DV. The provisional list of Nagata papers (1, 8, 107, 144, 150, 208, 287, 389) are all about different outcome associations; none specifically focus on school-hours phone use as the study's core construct. L1-L4 not satisfied for any specific corpus paper.

Title 'Social media potentially linked to depression in children' published May 22, 2025 maps to paper 8 (Nagata et al., JAMA Network Open, 2025 — social media use and depressive symptoms during early adolescence, ABCD). Paper 8 reports cross-lagged paths: SM Y1 -> depressive symptoms Y2, beta=0.07; Y2->Y3, beta=0.09. Article timing (May 2025) coincides with paper 8's publication in JAMA Network Open. 'Social media potentially linked to depression' paraphrases paper 8's core finding uniquely.

Title 'Addictive screen use tied to youth mental health risks' published June 19, 2025 maps to paper 3 (Xiao et al., JAMA 2025 — addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors, suicidal ideation, and mental health in US youths). 'Addictive screen use' is a term that uniquely characterizes paper 3 (which uses SMAQ and MPIQ trajectory groups for addictive social media and phone use). Paper 48 (Keyes — childhood symptoms predict screen time changes) does not have 'addictive screen use → mental health' framing. L3 satisfied for paper 3.

Title 'Social media use and binge eating in early adolescence' published January 6, 2025 maps precisely to paper 35 (Shi et al., Obesity, 2025 — concurrent and prospective associations of social media usage with binge eating symptoms in early adolescence from ABCD). Title is nearly verbatim restatement of paper 35's topic and finding. L3 uniquely satisfied — no other corpus paper specifically links social media use to binge eating in early adolescence.

exclusion_reason: general aggregator — weekly news digest covering peanut patch data, norovirus, and unrelated topics; no evidence this item covers paper 35 or any corpus paper about social media/screen time
evidence: Title 'Weekly review: New peanut patch data, norovirus outbreaks, and more' from Contemporary Pediatrics (Jan 13, 2025) is a general weekly digest. The title content (peanut patch, norovirus) has no overlap with any corpus paper's topic. Provisional assignment to paper 35 (social media + binge eating) appears to be a search artifact. L1-L4 not met.

exclusion_reason: out-of-corpus topic — article covers toddler/infant screen time and autism risk; no corpus paper examines screen time in children under 2 years or autism diagnosis as an outcome
evidence: Title 'Screen time under 2 years of age and autism risk at 12 years' describes a study of screen use in infants/toddlers and autism risk — out-of-corpus. Provisional paper 84 (Shou, Acta Psychologica — screen time + cognitive function + putamen volume in ABCD children 9-10) does not cover toddler age range or autism outcomes. L1-L4 not met for any corpus paper.

Title 'Study finds parents' screen habits shape kids' media exposure' published February 6, 2025 maps to paper 184 (Nagata et al., Pediatric Research, 2025 — associations between media parenting practices and early adolescent screen use, ABCD). Paper 184 examines how parental media habits (including parental bedroom screen use predicting problematic SM use: B=1.91) influence child screen behavior. Paraphrase 'parents' screen habits → kids' media exposure' uniquely matches paper 184's core finding.

Title 'Social media use linked to rising inattentive ADHD symptoms in children' published January 22, 2026 maps to papers 435/436 (Nivins et al., Pediatrics Open Science, 2025 — digital media, genetics, and risk for ADHD symptoms; social media use x time predicts inattention beta=0.03). Papers 435 and 436 share the same DOI (10.1542/pedsos.2025-000922) and represent the same paper. 'Inattentive ADHD symptoms' and 'social media' uniquely map to this paper. Paper 50 (Deng, online social activity → ADHD) is also possible but paper 435/436 more specifically aligns with 'inattentive' ADHD subtype phrasing.

Title 'Kids' Social Media Use Linked to Lower Reading and Memory Scores, Study Suggests' (Education Week, Oct 17, 2025). 'Memory scores' uniquely maps to paper 144 (Nagata et al., Lancet Regional Health-Americas 2026 — SM trajectories and spatial/verbal memory: B=-1.90 for RAVLT initial trials). 'Reading scores' may map to paper 1 (Nagata, JAMA 2025 — cognitive performance including oral reading recognition) or paper 144. The article may also reference paper 310 (Carvalho 2025 — crystallized performance includes verbal/reading tasks). Multi-mapped to papers 144 and 1 as the primary matches.

Title 'Screen Time Can Raise Children's Chance of OCD. Educators Can Help Prevent That' (Education Week, Dec 20, 2022) maps to paper 133 (Nagata et al., Journal of Adolescent Health, 2023 — screen time and OCD among children 9-10 years old, prospective cohort from ABCD). OCD as an outcome of screen time is a distinctive finding uniquely matching paper 133 in the corpus. Provisional paper 521 (Must, autism/obesity) is mismatched — that paper does not cover OCD. L3 satisfied for paper 133.

Title 'New study shows social media use predicted future depression in tweens' (Washington Post, June 11, 2025). Summary explicitly states 'data was drawn from the national Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development Study.' 'Social media use predicted future depression' with longitudinal framing maps precisely to paper 8 (Nagata et al., JAMA Network Open, 2025 — social media use and depressive symptoms, cross-lagged panel, beta=0.07-0.09 for SM->depression). Article date (June 2025) aligns with paper 8 publication. L3 uniquely satisfied.

Title 'Social media use triples depression symptoms for pre-teens: Study' (LiveNOW from FOX, May 23, 2025) published on the same day as other articles covering paper 8 (Nagata, JAMA Network Open, 2025 — social media use and depressive symptoms, ABCD). 'Triples depression symptoms' likely reflects a popular-press interpretation/exaggeration of paper 8's cross-lagged finding (beta=0.07-0.09, or possibly a subgroup difference). Article date (May 23, 2025) and topic align with paper 8 publication timing. L3 satisfied; confidence modestly reduced due to 'triples' claim being a strong quantitative assertion not directly traceable to paper 8's reported estimates.

Title 'Excessive screen time linked to manic symptoms in kids, study finds' (LiveNOW from FOX, March 5, 2025) maps uniquely to paper 49 (Nagata et al., Social Psychiatry and Psychiatric Epidemiology, 2025 — screen time and manic symptoms in early adolescents from ABCD; social media screen time B=0.20 for manic symptoms). 'Manic symptoms' is a highly distinctive outcome that uniquely identifies paper 49 among corpus papers. No other corpus paper specifically examines mania/manic symptoms as an outcome.

Title 'Prolonged social media use may reduce intelligence, study' (Jang, Oct 14, 2025) published same date as A0053 covering the same cluster of outlets reacting to paper 1 (Nagata et al., JAMA 2025 — social media trajectories and cognitive performance). 'Reduce intelligence' paraphrases paper 1's finding that high-increasing SM trajectory is associated with lower cognitive performance scores on NIH Toolbox. Paper 190 (Sauce 2022, Scientific Reports — digital media + intelligence) is older and less likely the target. Published October 2025 timing aligns with paper 1 press coverage wave.

Title 'Social media is designed to be addictive, jury finds. Research links excessive use to mental harm' (Science News, March 26, 2026). This is an aggregator article about the Meta/YouTube legal case plus research evidence. The research link to 'excessive use → mental harm' most distinctively maps to paper 3 (Xiao et al., JAMA 2025 — addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors/mental health). Paper 86 (Nagata, AJPM 2026 — problematic screen use → mental health) is also a possible match. Confidence reduced to 0.72 because this appears to be a broad aggregator with multiple sources; without access to full text, it is uncertain which specific corpus papers are cited. Provisional list includes papers 3 and 86.

Title 'Screen addiction affects teens' mental health. How to spot it, and help' (Science News, July 22, 2025) maps to paper 3 (Xiao et al., JAMA 2025 — addictive screen use trajectories and suicidal behaviors/suicidal ideation/mental health in US youths). 'Screen addiction → teens' mental health' paraphrases paper 3's core finding about addictive SM/phone use trajectory classes predicting mental health outcomes. Provisional paper 521 (Must, autism/obesity) is irrelevant. Paper 215 (Al-shoaibi, screen time + BMI + sleep) is not specifically about screen addiction. L3 satisfied for paper 3.
